newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Prime Minister Kengo forms Zaire crisis government.
newsitem.headline: Prime Minister Kengo forms Zaire crisis government.

text.p: President Mobutu Sese Seko signed a decree on Tuesday approving a new crisis cabinet to guide the war effort to retake land ethnic Tutsi rebels have seized in eastern Zaire.

He retained centrist Prime Minister Kengo wa Dondo, a part-Tutsi accused by radicals of weakness in the face of the rebellion, while most of the ministers in the outgoing 47-member cabinet were changed and radical opposition politicians were brought into the government for the first time.

But some members of both the pro-Mobutu FPC alliance and the radical opposition were crying foul, saying no consensus had been reached over the appointments and the decisions had been taken arbritrarily.
Kengo's spokesman Sombo Dibele said the new government took office in the Central African country as of Tuesday.

Moderate opposition member and interior minister Kamanda wa Kamanda is moved to the Foreign Ministry, and replaced by Mwando Nsimba, another moderate who previously was transport minister, according to the official list read on state television.

Grand Admiral Mavua Madima, the defence minister, is removed from office. His place goes to General Likulia Bolongo, former chief of military justice, one-time security chief and a close ally of Mobutu. He and Mobutu are from the same Equateur Region.
Three radical politicians entered the government, among them Lambert Mende, a long-term opponent of Mobutu who becomes deputy prime minister in charge of transport and communications.
Tshisbwabwa Ashila Pasi, a former ally of the main radical opposition leader Etienne Tshisekedi but who followed a breakaway faction earlier this year, becomes justice minister.
The number two in Mobutu's Popular Movement (MPR), Banza Mukalayi, becomes a deputy prime minister in charge of Zaire's key mines ministry.
Zaire's bickering politicians reached an accord on the new government after missing two deadlines set by the president.

Mobutu, who has ruled Zaire for 31 years, returned home last Tuesday after four months in Europe for cancer treatment. He vowed to crush the rebellion which erupted in October during his absence, and moved to reorganise the army and government.

Kyungu wa Kumwanza, president of a federalist party and a key figure in the mineral-rich Shaba Province, told Reuters he did not support the government and that his party would now withdraw from the FPC alliance.
"The desire of the people was to see Kengo and his government go. The expectations of the people have not been respected," Kyungu said.
The chief aide to Tshisekedi, Mobutu's main opponent in the radical opposition, said retaining Kengo as prime minister made a mockery of the desires of the majority of the population.

"These people are challenging the desire of the majority. Clearly they have no need for reconciliation. We cannot reconstruct the country with hatred, but in the days that come we will impose national reconciliation," Mukendi wa Mulumba told Reuters. He did not say how they intended to do this.

Tshiskedi was sacked as prime minister by Mobutu in 1993. He and his followers say that action was illegal as Tshisekedi was appopinted by a sovereign national congress. Radicals in Kinshasa's teeming workering class districts vowed trouble if he were not reappointed.
Mobutu flew out of Kinshasa early on Tuesday to spend Christmas in his jungle palace at Gbadolite in northern Zaire, his spokesman kabuya Lumuna said.
